summary: ARES-HUD brings Mars exploration into an interactive mission dashboard. Using real NASA imagery of Jezero crater, users plan hypothetical astronaut excursions, select science stops, simulate dust hazards, and recalculate routes back to their habitat. A simulated Sol timeline and independent tablet interface connect mission planning with a portable field experience. The project makes planetary data approachable while clearly distinguishing genuine observations from simulated mission conditions.
details:
How could an astronaut turn a map of Mars into an understandable exploration plan and adapt that plan when conditions change?

ARES-HUD explores this question through a browser-based mission-planning demonstrator. Built by Team Mar-tian, it combines authentic NASA orbital imagery, interactive route planning, simulated mission progress, and a compact tablet interface.

Planning on real Mars imagery

The surface planner uses NASA Mars Trek’s preliminary Jezero mosaic from the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter Context Camera. A hypothetical 4 km × 4 km exploration sector is registered to the imagery through its documented tile matrix. Users can pan and zoom, inspect coordinates and scale, and select or reorder hypothetical science stops.

Routes are calculated using deterministic A* across a 40 × 40 grid, with nominally 100-metre cells. The algorithm supports eight movement directions and prevents diagonal corner cutting through blocked cells. Users can introduce a simulated dust hazard, compare the original route with a detour, and select Return to Hab. When a route is blocked, the interface explicitly reports that it is unavailable.

From mission control to a field interface

Send to Tablet transfers a validated plan snapshot to a separate, compact interface. The tablet independently recalculates routes and supports its own dust, return, and reset controls. This demonstrates how a mission plan could move between a planning dashboard and a field display without requiring a backend.

Eight simulated Sol excursions provide playback, mission logs, and calculated route metrics. An optional simulated reconnaissance layer represents uncertainty in planning knowledge while keeping the genuine NASA imagery visible.

Exploration with transparent sources

A separate, interactive 3D Globe provides an illustrative overview and a transition into Jezero planning. Its procedural artwork is explicitly SIMULATED; it is not NASA imagery or a geographically registered planetary map.

The source inspector presents NASA orbital and Perseverance surface images alongside a USGS educational geological reference. The project distinguishes OBSERVED imagery, DERIVED coordinates and distances, INTERPRETED geological context, and SIMULATED mission assumptions.

Implementation and value

ARES-HUD uses React, JavaScript, Leaflet, Three.​js, and Vite, with static hosting through GitHub Pages. Its mission engines run locally, and cached imagery avoids dependence on live NASA services during use. Documented verification includes 39 passing automated tests and production-browser checks.

The project makes the relationship between planetary imagery, route choices, uncertainty, and mission interfaces accessible to students and space enthusiasts. It demonstrates a planning workflow rather than operational navigation: hazards, costs, astronaut locations, and schedules are simulated. Numerical elevation, slope analysis, live telemetry, and astronaut-safety predictions are not implemented.

Hackathon planning demonstrator. Routes and hazards are simulated; not flight-qualified navigation.
